title: Yennicock / Yennicott (Southold)
summary: Yennicock, Yennicott, Yenycott, and related spellings appear in seventeenth-century records for the North Fork. William Wallace Tooker later argued that the name described a broader tract from the Peconic River to Plum Gut, not only the modern Southold village area.
activity_update_summary: Added a source-grounded introduction explaining the recorded Yennicock and Yennicott spelling variants, Tooker's broader North Fork interpretation, and the uncertainty surrounding his proposed translation.
why_this_matters: The variants Yennycok, Yenycott, Yeanocock, and others show how one Indigenous place-name was repeatedly reshaped in colonial spelling. Tooker's wider North Fork interpretation also warns against shrinking an Indigenous geography to the boundaries of a later town. Preserving both the variants and the uncertainty lets visitors see a layered record rather than treating one spelling or marker as final.
introduction_title: A place-name larger than Southold village
introduction_content: Seventeenth-century records preserve Yennicock, Yennicott, Yennycok, Yenycott, Yenicott, Yeanocock, Yannocock, and Yeannecock for places on the North Fork. William Wallace Tooker traced the earliest form he found to an October 25, 1640 record concerning Richard Jackson's house. He also argued that the name could refer broadly to the peninsula between the Peconic River and Plum Gut and to Native people planting at Aquebogue—not only to today's Southold village. Tooker interpreted the word as “at the extended land or country,” but that is his 1911 linguistic reconstruction, not a confirmed Corchaug translation. The marker therefore provides modern orientation while the record points to a larger and less fixed geographic scope.
history_content: According to Tooker, the earliest occurrence he found was an October 25, 1640 Southold record referring to Richard Jackson “of Yennacock.” He listed recorded variants from 1642 through 1668 and argued that some records used the name for a much wider tract than the Southold village locality. That geographic conclusion is Tooker's interpretation of colonial records; the map marker remains an approximate modern reference point.
translation_content:
William Wallace Tooker compared Yennicock or Yeannecock with a Massachusetts form and interpreted it as “at the extended land or country.” This is an early twentieth-century linguistic reconstruction based on comparative evidence, not a confirmed translation from a surviving Corchaug speaker or community source. It should therefore be read as attributed and provisional.

Why Place Names Matter

“Place-naming reflects Indigenous laws, governance systems, and relationships to land, water, and territory.”

— Yellowhead Institute, The Right to Reclaim a Name (2026), Factsheet opening statement
preservation_content: The history preserves Yennicock/Yennicott as a North Fork place-name while keeping uncertainty about its exact extent visible.
whereintheworld_content: Approximate blue/general placement at Southold village on the North Fork. Coordinates are approximate and do not define the broader historic area.
